brief.summary: The author argues that Lebanon must finally assert its sovereignty over Hezbollah. Citing the interception of roughly half a tonne of TNT and C4 bound for Beirut's southern suburbs, the piece notes that Hezbollah now openly claims the explosives and demands their return, unlike its past denials over similar explosives used in assassinations such as Rafik Hariri's. The authors suggest this boldness may reflect sympathisers inside the government and security services. They reject the claim that Hezbollah's arms protect the Shiite community as a pretext, and describe the group as an Iranian proxy rather than a Lebanese party. They say its ties to smuggling and organised crime have built a parallel economy that undermines state institutions and turns Lebanon into an arena for foreign interference, with citizens bearing the cost of wars that brought loss and isolation. The excerpt is an opinion piece, and its recommendations are not visible in the text provided.
brief.argument: Lebanon must assert state sovereignty over Hezbollah, which the author describes as an Iranian proxy whose arms and criminal networks undermine the state.

9ec052d64b60de63.title: Israeli voters have largely moved on from October 7
9ec052d64b60de63.summary: Israeli voters have largely moved on from October 7 newspress_en Tue, 10/20/2026 - 04:38 Opinion Israel’s upcoming elections are widely regarded as particularly consequential—not only for Israel itself, but for the region as a whole. The past three years, since October 7, followed by the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, have been unprecedented in almost every respect. Yet all those fronts remain volatile. Within Israel, the political picture is remarkably confusing, even…

brief.summary: The authors argue that Israel's upcoming elections, though widely seen as consequential, have returned to a pre-October 7 political pattern, with the two blocs roughly evenly matched in polling (which they caution must be treated carefully). They contend that the elections centre less on October 7 or the Iran confrontation than on the character of Israeli society, divisions that predate the war, and the judicial overhaul. Netanyahu's coalition has largely pushed accountability for October 7 out of voters' calculations. The authors attribute this to two factors: a trauma that cut across political lines and hardened attitudes toward Palestinians, and a deep perception that Israel faces an existential struggle, which the Iran war reinforced. They conclude the contest is effectively a referendum on Netanyahu, framed as "Only Bibi" versus "Anyone but Bibi".
brief.argument: Israel's elections are turning on pre-war societal divisions and the judicial overhaul rather than on October 7 accountability, because trauma and a sense of existential threat have pushed that accountability out of voters' calculations.
brief.turkey: For Türkiye, an electoral contest that is largely a referendum on Netanyahu, with a hardened public mood on Palestinians and the Iran confrontation, suggests continuity in Israeli regional posture regardless of the outcome.

ai.sum: An opinion piece argues Israeli voters have largely moved past October 7 ahead of elections seen as consequential regionally.

1d051292d54362dc.title: Trump’s diesel deal has no winners
1d051292d54362dc.summary: Trump’s diesel deal has no winners newspress_en Tue, 10/20/2026 - 04:24 Business & Economy President Donald Trump’s controversial decision to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel exports won’t do much, if anything, to lower fuel prices, especially before next month’s midterm elections. Yet it won’t provide Moscow with a financial windfall, either. The administration’s surprise suspension of bans on Russian diesel exports, announced on Friday, faces legal and political…

brief.summary: The authors argue that Trump's suspension of sanctions on Russian diesel exports will do little to lower fuel prices before the midterms, while also giving Moscow no real financial windfall. They note the waiver faces legal challenges under 2022 legislation barring Russian fossil fuel imports and a growing bipartisan backlash in Congress. The piece contends the deal was paired with a demand for an energy ceasefire that would strip Ukraine of its most effective weapon, long-range strikes on Russian refineries, which have sharply cut Russian diesel output and export earnings. Ukraine has complied with a pause on energy strikes since 10 October, but Russia has not accepted a ceasefire, and Kyiv has lost some Starlink military access. The authors conclude that Russia could still easily supply the volumes envisaged, so the deal delivers little benefit to anyone.
brief.argument: Trump's diesel waiver has no winners: it will not meaningfully cut fuel prices, offers Moscow no windfall, and costs Ukraine its most effective energy-pressure tool.
recommendations: Rescind the diesel waiver, as a bipartisan group of senators has requested
Keep Ukraine's long-range strikes on Russian refineries as a means of limiting Russian energy revenue

ai.sum: Trump administration suspended sanctions on Russian diesel exports, a move analysts say will not meaningfully lower fuel prices.

6b2084bedfbb4999.title: Egypt’s economy better equipped to absorb disruptions
6b2084bedfbb4999.summary: Egypt’s economy better equipped to absorb disruptions newspress_en Tue, 10/20/2026 - 09:23 Infographics Record remittances, stronger investment inflows and higher foreign reserves are giving Egypt’s economy greater room to absorb shocks, but sustaining the recovery will depend on addressing financial imbalances and accelerating economic reforms. Egypt found itself better equipped to absorb disruptions caused by the latest regional turmoil than it was four years ago, when…

brief.summary: The authors argue that Egypt is better placed than in 2022 to absorb external shocks. Real GDP growth reached 5.1% in fiscal 2025/2026, with record remittances, tourism, and rising foreign direct investment supporting foreign currency inflows. Reserves hit $57.3bn in September 2026, a larger buffer against volatility. The piece is careful to say this is not a structural fix: the recovery depends on correcting financial imbalances and speeding up economic reforms. It also notes that the Suez Canal remains far below record levels despite a 23% rise in revenue to $4.67bn, since Houthi attacks in the Red Sea from late 2023 pushed shipping around the Cape of Good Hope and cut canal traffic and revenue. Tourism is projected to exceed $20bn in 2026 despite regional tensions.
brief.argument: Egypt's stronger inflows and reserves give it more room to absorb regional shocks, but sustaining this depends on fixing financial imbalances and accelerating reforms.
recommendations: Address financial imbalances in the economy
Accelerate economic reforms to sustain the recovery

b1a5a50b93b578ea.title: Guns, Growth, and the German Reinvention of Military Keynesianism
b1a5a50b93b578ea.summary: In March 2025, Germany did more than loosen a fiscal rule. It fused two national emergencies — a deteriorating European security order and a deteriorating industrial model — into a single constitutional bargain. The reform de facto exempted German defense expenditure from any domestic budgetary ceiling — as the German Bundesbank itself has acknowledged — and enabled a military expansion of extraordinary proportions. E.U. debt rules of 3 percent of GDP for annual government…

brief.summary: The authors argue that Germany's March 2025 constitutional change, which effectively exempted defence spending from the debt brake, was a logroll: security conservatives, Social Democrats and Greens each traded support for their priorities, with the spending justified in shared security and modernisation terms. They link it to 'China Shock 2.0', as Chinese overcapacity hits German industry, and note that defence procurement overlaps with the capabilities that sector needs. Drawing on the American rearmament of 1950-53, they say military Keynesianism works best when the spending absorbs slack, goes to a net arms exporter, and drives frontier technology. Germany meets some preconditions but its procurement is still weighted to conventional platforms, with frontier-tech shares falling. Procurement rules such as the 25 million euro Bundestag approval threshold and a risk-averse culture block innovation. They conclude Germany has a coalition but not yet a growth strategy.
brief.argument: Germany's defence buildup has become a politically durable military-Keynesian logroll, but without a deliberate innovation-focused procurement strategy it will cushion industrial decline rather than restore growth.
recommendations: Link military procurement explicitly to an industrial strategy aimed at innovation and productivity
Raise the 25 million euro Bundestag approval threshold or otherwise ease approval for innovative contracts
Provide long-term demand signals so that successful prototypes can scale and escape the 'valley of death'
Shift a larger share of spending toward frontier and dual-use technologies

ai.sum: War on the Rocks analyses Germany's March 2025 fiscal reform exempting defence spending from budget ceilings.

86b191209bc8d527.title: Nature Credits: Europe’s Next Financial Crime Blind Spot
86b191209bc8d527.summary: Brussels is designing a nature credits market with integrity rules but none on money laundering; its own carbon market shows what that gap can cost.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the European Commission's emerging nature credits market is being designed with integrity rules but no anti-money-laundering safeguards, a gap they call the next financial crime blind spot. They compare it with the EU carbon market, where fraud losses led to fixes only after the damage, and note that the Commission's July 2025 Roadmap never mentions fraud, money laundering or crime. Drawing on Interpol's typology of carbon-market crime, they say nature credits face the same risks, with measurement of outcomes and laundering through landholders in areas of environmental crime as the most acute. They stress that the market is still small, which makes it cheap to secure now, and propose three steps: add brokers, registries and verifiers to the Anti-Money Laundering Regulation's obliged entities, build identity and anti-double-counting checks into the registry before recognition, and run a financial crime risk assessment before the 2027 governance advice.
brief.argument: Europe is building a nature credits market with integrity rules but no anti-money-laundering safeguards, and it should close that gap now, before the market grows, rather than after losses as with the carbon market.
recommendations: Add brokers, registries and verifiers of EU-recognised nature credits to the obliged entities of the Anti-Money Laundering Regulation, with simplified due diligence for smallholders.
Write customer identification, beneficial ownership checks, sanctions screening, unique serial numbers and cross-registry double-issuance checks into the federated registry before recognition.
Conduct a financial crime risk assessment with Europol and financial intelligence units before the 2027 governance advice.
Require methodologies to show that outcome claims can be re-checked from primary field evidence by someone other than the seller.

ai.sum: RUSI warns that the EU's nature credits market lacks money laundering integrity rules, risking financial crime.

It assembles news photographs from 15 to 19 October 2026 across several regions: protests in Paris and Tirana against the cost of living and rising fuel prices, daily life in Beirut, displacement camps in Gaza, wildfires in California, and scenes in Brazil, Cairo and New Zealand. 643a6d1cc2b12e63.title: Egypt 2025-26 economy: resilience amid challenges
643a6d1cc2b12e63.summary: Egypt 2025-26 economy: resilience amid challenges newspress_en Tue, 10/20/2026 - 09:23 Infographics Record remittances, stronger investment inflows and higher foreign reserves are giving Egypt’s economy greater room to absorb shocks, but sustaining the recovery will depend on addressing financial imbalances and accelerating economic reforms. Egypt found itself better equipped to absorb disruptions caused by the latest regional turmoil than it was four years ago, when the…

brief.summary: The authors argue that Egypt's economy is better placed to absorb regional shocks than it was four years ago, when the Russia-Ukraine war exposed distortions in the foreign exchange market and caused a dollar shortage. They point to 5.1% real GDP growth, record remittances, tourism and foreign direct investment inflows, and foreign reserves of $57.3bn in September 2026 as the main sources of this buffer. They note that the Suez Canal remains well below its record revenues, which peaked near $10.25bn in 2023, because Houthi attacks in the Red Sea forced rerouting around the Cape of Good Hope. Their conclusion is that this resilience does not amount to overcoming structural weaknesses, and that sustaining recovery depends on fixing financial imbalances and accelerating economic reform.
brief.argument: Egypt's external buffers have strengthened, but the recovery is not yet secure without addressing financial imbalances and speeding up structural reform.
recommendations: Address the financial imbalances that still weigh on the economy
Accelerate economic reforms to sustain the recovery
brief.turkey: The Red Sea disruption that cut Suez Canal revenues is a reminder of how Houthi shipping attacks hit regional economies, a point relevant to Türkiye's own maritime and corridor exposure.

ai.sum: Al Majalla reports Egypt's economy is better placed to absorb shocks thanks to record remittances, investment and reserves.

a92aea515387d333.title: New CFR Book by Charles A. Kupchan Provides a Guide to Building Order in a Multipolar World
a92aea515387d333.summary: “The stable and open international order erected during America’s watch—Pax Americana—is unraveling, giving way to global disarray,” writes Charles A. Kupchan, senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), in his new book, Bringing Order to Anarchy: Governing the World to Come. “A constructive and sustained dialogue about the order that comes next has […]

brief.summary: The authors, through Charles A. Kupchan's new book, argue that the American-led order is unraveling and that the world is entering uncharted multipolar territory in which power is diffusing. They contend that order must be built both from the bottom up, through devolution of authority to regions, and from the top down, because interdependence still demands central governance. To get around the paralysis of the United Nations and similar bodies, Kupchan proposes a network of great-power steering groups modelled on the nineteenth-century Concert of Europe, bringing democracies and autocracies to the same table to set aside differences over domestic governance. He insists the work starts at home: democracies must first show they can deliver for their citizens and outperform illiberal alternatives, which requires a new social contract for the digital era.
brief.argument: A stable post-American order can only be built through regional devolution combined with a concert of great powers that cooperates across ideological lines, and democracies must first renew their domestic social contracts.
recommendations: Establish concert-style great-power steering groups, including democracies and autocracies, to oversee global governance.
Devolve authority and responsibility to regions while retaining centralised governance where interdependence requires it.
Forge a new social contract for the digital era to restore democratic performance at home.

ai.sum: CFR publishes Charles Kupchan's book on building order in a multipolar world after the unravelling of Pax Americana.

e5ed60f851191c52.title: A Canadian west coast oil pipeline and coalitional oil security in a Taiwan contingency
e5ed60f851191c52.summary: Canadian oil imports can provide insurance and reliability for East Asian countries amid the instability of oil supply from the Middle East. The post A Canadian west coast oil pipeline and coalitional oil security in a Taiwan contingency appeared first on Atlantic Council .

brief.summary: The authors argue that the US-Israeli war with Iran is undermining old assumptions about oil security, making Western Canadian crude delivered through the Pacific Link pipeline an attractive hedge for East Asian democracies. They contend Canadian supply is politically aligned, avoids vulnerable maritime chokepoints, and reaches the region faster than alternatives, though economic hurdles remain. They propose coker retrofits at existing refineries in Japan, Taiwan and South Korea to process heavy oil sands crude, a process they estimate would take four to five years, and note South Korean refiners could take existing Canadian exports with little change. They also argue that Taipei and Tokyo should prioritise oil security over cost, given the rising risk of an energy quarantine or blockade, and treat non-Middle Eastern crude as insurance against instability in the Persian Gulf and Bab el-Mandeb.
brief.argument: Western Canadian crude via the Pacific Link pipeline offers East Asian democracies a secure, faster-shipped supply hedge that should be valued above cost in a Taiwan contingency.
recommendations: Invest in coker retrofits at existing Japanese, Taiwanese and South Korean refineries to process Canadian heavy oil sands crude.
Accelerate South Korean refinery imports of Canadian crude, which need little or no retrofitting.
Revise energy security assumptions so that Taipei and Tokyo weight oil security above cost.
Treat non-Middle Eastern crude as insurance against Persian Gulf and Bab el-Mandeb disruption.

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analyses a Canadian west coast oil pipeline as supply security for East Asia in a Taiwan contingency.

090c5947798a1dff.title: Russia and the West Need a Future Beyond Vladimir Putin
090c5947798a1dff.summary: Russia and the West Need a Future Beyond Vladimir Putin bbert@hudson.org Tue, 10/20/2026 - 09:46 SVG Commentary Oct 20, 2026 Hudson Institute Russia and the West Need a Future Beyond Vladimir Putin John P. Walters President and CEO John P. Walters Commentary Caption Russia’s President Vladimir Putin attends a meeting with Russia’s Sports Minister in Moscow on October 20, 2026. (Getty Images) Toggle Table of Contents Contents Contents Share to Twitter Twitter Share to…

brief.summary: The authors argue that Western policy wrongly treats Vladimir Putin as indispensable to peace, when his war in Ukraine has in fact produced strategic failure for him and weakened Russia internally. They contend Ukraine's resilience and drones have imposed heavy costs and that escalation by Moscow is the desperate move of a losing side. Because Putin's rule depends on continued war, they conclude no negotiated peace is possible while he remains in power. They recommend decisive support for Ukraine, reinforced deterrence including repositioned nuclear-capable forces, and quiet channels to Russian elites, including some oligarchs, to prepare for a post-Putin Russia. The piece presents Putin's removal as necessary to halt aggression and to stop deeper Russian alignment with China.
brief.argument: Putin's war has produced strategic failure for him, so no negotiated peace is possible while he remains in power, and the West should back Ukraine decisively while preparing for a post-Putin Russia.
recommendations: Strengthen Ukraine decisively with military, economic and diplomatic assistance
Reposition nuclear-capable forces to reinforce deterrence
Expand channels to Russian elites capable of advancing change, including some oligarchs
Impose the new, stronger American economic sanctions already on the books

ai.sum: A Hudson Institute commentary argues Russia and the West need a future beyond Vladimir Putin.

39699435fc43e75d.title: The European Union as a compound power in Cold War 2.0
39699435fc43e75d.summary: Contrary to the prevailing narrative, the European Union has the economic power and strategic vision to act as a credible major power. Willingness to act is the missing piece. The post The European Union as a compound power in Cold War 2.0 appeared first on Atlantic Council .

brief.summary: The authors argue that the EU is usually read as a declining project, but that its structural assets already make it a credible compound power in the emerging Cold War 2.0. They point to the EU's position as the largest external trader, its high-complexity export base, its large net savings position, and the single market's coercive leverage. They locate the main constraint on European agency in institutional conversion of strategy into action, not in capacity. They trace a strategic awakening through the Niinistö report, Macron's Sorbonne speech and the Draghi competitiveness review, and frame the EU's energy shift away from Russian gas and its rebuilding of a defence industrial base as evidence of that capacity. The paper treats enlargement, especially toward Ukraine, Moldova and the Western Balkans, as the EU's most powerful long-term instrument.
brief.argument: The EU already has the economic power, strategic vision and structural assets to act as a compound power, so only its willingness to act constrains European agency.
recommendations: Complete the Capital Markets Union to channel European savings into European productive investment.
Defend and strategically deploy the EU's trade surplus through market access conditionality.
Expand the single market and membership or associate membership to Ukraine, Moldova, Iceland and the Western Balkans.
Align industrial policy with economic-security objectives through the CHIPS, Critical Raw Materials and Net-Zero Industry Acts, and deepen the single market in services and capital.
brief.turkey: The paper's enlargement and industrial-base arguments bear on Türkiye's relations with the EU and on the EU defence-industrial ecosystem Türkiye would interact with, though it does not address Türkiye directly.

ai.sum: Atlantic Council argues the EU has the economic power to act as a major power in Cold War 2.0 but lacks willingness.

1baabf20e6163f5d.title: President John F. Kennedy Fakes a Fever—The Cuban Missile Crisis, Day Five
1baabf20e6163f5d.summary: JFK pleaded illness to cancel a Midwest campaign trip and return to Washington to decide how to respond to the Cuban Missile Crisis.

brief.summary: The authors, through a retrospective by CFR senior fellow James M. Lindsay, recount Day Five of the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis. Kennedy cited a fever to cancel a Midwest campaign tour and return to Washington for an ExComm meeting. Advisers debated a naval blockade, which McNamara favoured as less escalatory, against an air strike pressed by Taylor and Bundy, who argued time favoured Moscow. Discussion also covered a hybrid blockade-then-strike option and whether to trade the Jupiter missiles in Turkey or Guantánamo. Kennedy ordered preparations for a blockade while keeping an air-strike option open within 48 to 72 hours, and began drafting a public address. The piece is a historical narrative, not a policy argument, and it is presented as a resurfaced essay first published in 2012.
brief.argument: Kennedy's feigned illness and his hedged order, a blockade with a strike option kept open, reflected the trade-offs his advisers debated on Day Five of the crisis.
brief.turkey: The piece notes that the U.S. Jupiter missiles in Turkey were discussed as a possible bargaining chip, a historical precedent for later debates over Türkiye's role in great-power crisis bargaining.

ai.sum: CFR recounts President Kennedy feigning illness to return to Washington during the Cuban Missile Crisis.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the transatlantic alliance has shifted from a quasi-theological faith into a hard-headed partnership grounded in concrete interests, a change prompted by Donald Trump but sustained by a broad conservative consensus. They point to the Hague pledge of 5 percent of GDP for defence by 2035, rising European spending, and Germany's rearmament as evidence that Europe is building real military power. They identify three conservative strands (restrainers, prioritizers focused on China, and Reaganite internationalists) that disagree on much but converge on wanting a self-defending Europe, judging alliances by results, and rejecting a return to the old order. The authors criticise EU measures such as the SAFE loan programme's European-content requirement and tech-sovereignty steering of cloud and AI contracts as a drift toward a "Fortress Europe" that would be self-defeating and would benefit Beijing. Their remedy is co-production and joint ventures rather than protectionism.
brief.argument: The alliance has lost its theology and gained a sturdier, interest-based partnership, but Europe risks undermining it by shutting out American defence industry.
recommendations: Pursue co-production and joint ventures with American firms rather than protectionist content rules
Buy the most capability in the shortest time, especially in missile defence, advanced aircraft, space and secure cloud and AI
Avoid steering public cloud and AI contracts toward European providers on sovereignty grounds
Stop waiting for a restoration of the pre-Trump Atlantic order and build European capacity now

brief.summary: The authors argue that the United States should refuse Iran's offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart nuclear talks in exchange for lifting the naval blockade, waiving oil sanctions and releasing frozen assets. They frame the offer as extortion rather than diplomacy, since Iran closed the waterway itself. They urge Washington to keep open the option of resuming bombing after the midterms, combined with economic pressure from the blockade and Treasury measures, which they say are a prelude to force. Drawing on Thomas Schelling's coercion theory, they argue that the credible threat of future pain, not pain already inflicted, is what produces bargaining leverage, and that Iran's offer aimed to end the current pressure before the threatened escalation arrived.

Pair military threat with the blockade and Treasury's Operation Economic Outcast so economic strain makes Iranian losses harder to absorb.

brief.summary: This podcast episode, hosted by Ilva Tare with Ivana Korajlić of Transparency International Bosnia and Herzegovina, examines Bosnia's October 2026 general election. The authors note the first use of biometric voter identification and optical scanners to curb fraud, and the first vote since Washington lifted sanctions on Milorad Dodik's network. Turnout fell to a record low of about 40 percent and most major parties lost votes, yet nationalist parties won in all three communities. Dodik's and Čović's parties will both sit in the state presidency, with both leaders saying neither will govern without the other. The discussion questions whether technology reduced fraud or merely shifted it to pre-election hiring and public spending, whether anyone has been held accountable for past irregularities, and whether EU conditionality still works given the stalled accession path.
brief.argument: Bosnia's election reforms did not break the nationalist deadlock, and fraud and accountability problems may simply have shifted rather than disappeared.

brief.argument: Türkiye is navigating overlapping regional crises shaped by US distraction, new defence arrangements, and strained partnerships, and the authors judge that some of its steps, such as the Libya ratification, have paid off.
brief.turkey: The piece frames the Mecca defence pact's ratification and a possible Saudi support role against the Houthis as direct decisions for Ankara, and it treats Azerbaijan and Israel as diplomatic files Türkiye must manage.

1c64c4b956aebb52.title: Canadian west coast oil as a hedge for East Asian energy security
1c64c4b956aebb52.summary: Canadian oil imports can provide insurance and reliability for East Asian countries amid the instability of oil supply from the Middle East. The post Canadian west coast oil as a hedge for East Asian energy security appeared first on Atlantic Council .

brief.summary: The authors argue that the US-Israeli war with Iran has undermined older assumptions about oil security, pushing East Asian importers to reconsider supply. They present Western Canadian crude, moved through the Pacific Link pipeline, as a hedge: Canada is a stable democracy, its exports reach the Pacific without passing through vulnerable chokepoints, and voyages to the region are much shorter. They acknowledge economic hurdles. Their practical proposals are coker retrofits at refineries in Japan, Taiwan and South Korea to process heavy sands crude, and faster uptake of existing Canadian imports, especially in South Korea. They also say Taipei and Tokyo should weight oil security above cost, given the rising risk of an energy quarantine or blockade around the Persian Gulf and Bab el-Mandeb.
brief.argument: Western Canadian oil via the Pacific Link pipeline offers East Asian democracies a secure, chokepoint-free supply hedge against Gulf instability, even at some economic cost.
recommendations: Invest in coker retrofits at East Asian refineries to process Canadian heavy oil sands crude
Accelerate South Korean imports of existing Canadian crude
Prioritise oil security over cost in crude sourcing, especially for Taiwan and Japan
Treat non-Middle Eastern crude as insurance against Persian Gulf and Bab el-Mandeb disruption

ai.sum: Atlantic Council argues Canadian west coast oil could hedge East Asian energy security against Middle East supply instability.

They argue that the key to analysis is spotting what is new in the rhetoric and working out why it changed. Since 2023, shifts first visible in rhetoric have been reinforced by policy and institutional moves: North Korea has abandoned the unification framework toward Seoul, calling it the 'most hostile state' and removing unification from its party charter and constitution. Its ties with Russia have moved from the 'strategic and tactical cooperation' language, once associated with China, to a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty, with troops and weapons sent to support Russia's war in Ukraine. The authors attribute these shifts to Pyongyang's growing confidence in its nuclear capabilities, its reassessment of the strategic value of the United States, and opportunities created by the Russian war. The piece is a members-only excerpt, so the full set of recommendations is not available.
brief.argument: North Korea's propaganda shifts since 2023 are early signals of institutionalised policy changes, driven by nuclear confidence, a reassessment of the US, and opportunities from the Russia-Ukraine war.

285e4abdea6bdb00.summary: America and Europe: A Blueprint for the Next Chapter bbert@hudson.org Tue, 10/20/2026 - 08:33 SVG Commentary Oct 20, 2026 Hudson Institute America and Europe: A Blueprint for the Next Chapter Peter Rough Senior Fellow and Director, Center on Europe and Eurasia Ulrich Speck Senior Fellow (Nonresident), Center on Europe and Eurasia Peter Rough & Ulrich Speck Commentary Caption The flags of NATO and its member states wave in Brussels, Belgium, on March 6, 2025. (Getty Images)…

brief.summary: The authors, writing for the Hudson Institute, argue that China, Russia, Iran and North Korea form an 'axis of challengers' seeking to dismantle the US-led order, and that the West has been slow to recognise this after a post-Cold War strategy of engagement failed. They reject a Kissinger-style strategy of splitting Beijing from Moscow, arguing the two are now too closely aligned. Instead they call for renewing the West through three tasks: a new defence division of labour in which Europe takes on most conventional defence against Russia while the US keeps a troop presence and nuclear umbrella (NATO 3.0), a common transatlantic technological-economic space covering AI and critical minerals, and a geopolitical triangle linking the US, Europe and Asian partners such as Japan, South Korea, India, Australia and the Philippines. The piece presents this as a response to a threat of a possible multi-front war.
brief.argument: The US and Europe must rebuild a united West through a new defence division of labour, a shared technology and economic space, and a triangle with Asian partners, because China and Russia now form a coherent anti-Western axis.
recommendations: Shift conventional defence against Russia to European allies while the US keeps meaningful troop presence and the nuclear umbrella during the transition
Build a common US-European technological-economic space that guards against technology leakage and dependence on Chinese supply chains
Expand existing frameworks such as the EU-US Trade and Technology Council, the Minerals Security Partnership and the G7
Make Japan, South Korea, India, Australia and the Philippines equal stakeholders in a Eurasian-scope Western response
brief.turkey: The proposed NATO 3.0 burden shift and Eurasian triangle would reshape the alliance environment in which Türkiye operates, with Europe carrying more conventional defence and Russia-facing responsibility.

763b35e1b1dc8578.title: Central Bank Currency Swaps Tracker
763b35e1b1dc8578.summary: This interactive map tracks central bank currency swaps from the financial crisis of 2007 through the COVID-19 pandemic and into the present, focusing on the swap arrangements of the three largest central banks—the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank, and the People’s Bank of China.

brief.summary: The authors trace the evolution of central bank currency swap lines from the 2007-08 financial crisis through the COVID-19 shock to the present, focusing on the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the People's Bank of China. They explain the mechanics of swaps, noting that most lines are de facto unidirectional and that some are backed by treasuries rather than central banks. They show the Fed's lines as crisis-driven tools that filled dollar funding gaps and now look near-permanent, the ECB's lines as a mix of swaps and repo facilities for periphery and non-euro states, and the PBoC's network as a steadily widening tool used mainly to prop up indebted developing countries, often through rolling short-term RMB drawings that sit outside normal debt disclosure. The authors conclude that the permanence of Fed and ECB lines may encourage currency mismatches in banks, while PBoC lines let governments defer structural adjustment.
brief.argument: Permanent Fed and ECB swap lines risk encouraging bank currency mismatches, while the PBoC's rolling swaps let governments defer balance-of-payments adjustment, so tighter limits on short-term bank funding and liquid local-currency asset requirements matter more.
recommendations: Restrain banks' reliance on short-term foreign-currency funding
Require foreign banks to hold high-quality, liquid local-currency assets
Bring short-term rolling swap drawings within international debt disclosure requirements
brief.turkey: The UAE's 2022 local-currency swap line with Türkiye is cited as an example of a Gulf state using swaps to build ties with a heavily indebted economy, which bears on Türkiye's external financing options.

brief.summary: The article, published by Al Majalla, reports that the Islamic State plans to sharply step up attacks in Iraq in the coming months to spread fear after the US-led coalition's late-September withdrawal. It describes a recent run of incidents, including a foiled suicide attack in Pirdi on the Kirkuk-Erbil road and attacks on Federal Police, army and Popular Mobilisation Forces units in Kirkuk and Hawija. The authors argue IS has found refuge in the 'fragile regions' of northern Diyala, Kirkuk and Nineveh, which are disputed between Baghdad and Iraqi Kurdistan and lack a political framework for joint security. They attribute this to unresolved disputed-territory issues, sectarian and ethnic manipulation, and the region's proximity to Iran and Syria. The piece reports that Iraqi authorities have moved toward closer Peshmerga, army and security cooperation, and cites an analyst arguing that Article 140 can no longer be deferred.
brief.argument: IS is exploiting unresolved disputes between Baghdad and Erbil over the northern 'fragile regions' to mount an escalating campaign in Iraq after the coalition's withdrawal.
recommendations: Resolve the disputed-territories question, with Article 140 implementation no longer deferred
Make the joint Iraqi army and Peshmerga brigades fully operational and able to control the areas between their positions
Defuse sectarian and ethnic manipulation in Diyala, Nineveh and Kirkuk
brief.turkey: An IS resurgence along the Kirkuk-Erbil corridor and the Iraqi-Syrian border zone would bear on Türkiye's Iraq border security and on Kurdish-Arab-Turkmen tensions in Kirkuk, where Turkmen interests are directly involved.

It suggests that the past may survive in an image—or a collection of images—that can be revisited, or at least recognised, centuries later. Yet standing before the works, with their…

brief.summary: The authors, writing in Al Majalla, read Yasmina Nysten's Beirut exhibition Memory Keepers as a meditation on memory's elusiveness rather than its preservation. They argue the turquoise-toned oil portraits present fragments and suspended scenes that blur personal experience with collective or imagined memory. Nysten, they note, pursues portraiture beyond literal likeness, building narratives that begin and then withdraw. Her open-ended compositions, such as a girl asleep over a book or three women studying a map, leave questions unresolved so that what might happen next stays possible. The piece is an art review with no policy content, so the analysis is framed around aesthetic intent rather than strategic argument.
brief.argument: Nysten's paintings use fragmentary, open-ended scenes to show memory as an uncertain concept rather than a preserved record.

c923425e577e3fb5.title: Tehran is a Different Beast Now
c923425e577e3fb5.summary: The Tehran that the world knew is gone. It died in the fires with former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei on the first day of the war in February. His son and new Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei — wherever he is and in whatever physical condition — witnessed his father, wife, and other close family members die in the same airstrike that wounded him. The White House believed that the conflict would last only a few weeks, but the Islamic Republic has proven less fragile than…

brief.summary: The author, a former CIA analyst, argues that Iran's leadership has shifted into a harder-line 'New Tehran' mindset after the February decapitation strikes that killed Ali Khamenei and much of his family. Rather than treating Iranian behaviour as factional chaos, the piece reads it as strategically coherent: surviving leaders see themselves as 'dead men walking', judge that Ali Khamenei's caution cost him his life, and believe only an aggressive posture that imposes costs can deter further attacks. The author says Iran is using control of the Strait of Hormuz, the threat to Gulf infrastructure and the expectation that US economic pressure will wear down Washington, while relying on Russia and China for support. The piece concludes that Washington has misread Tehran, that a 'Old Tehran' return would show up as acceptance of a simple blockade-for-blockade ceasefire, and it closes by proposing creative multilateral diplomacy as a way out.
brief.argument: Iran's behaviour reflects a deliberate harder-line strategic reassessment by a new leadership that sees aggressive brinkmanship as its only route to survival, and Washington's misreading of this is trapping US policy.
recommendations: Recalibrate US assumptions to treat Iran's posture as strategically coherent rather than erratic
Explore imaginative multilateral arrangements that address Iran's security fears and assure it against renewed war
Avoid expecting factional rifts in Tehran to ease the US dilemma

ai.sum: An analysis argues Iran has changed fundamentally after Ali Khamenei was killed in February and Mojtaba Khamenei became Supreme Leader.

90d82915b50bee84.title: Neue EU-Strategie: Ein eigener Plan für die Arktis
90d82915b50bee84.summary: Was in der Arktis klimatisch, wirtschaftlich und militärisch geschieht, ist von enormer Bedeutung für Europa - dieser Erkenntnis will die EU nun Taten folgen lassen. Heute will sie eine Strategie für die Region vorstellen.

brief.summary: The piece, an SWP commentary, argues that the Arctic has become a major arena for Europe because melting ice opens new shipping routes, eases access to oil, gas, metals and rare earths, and raises military competition, with Russia reactivating Soviet-era sites and the US expanding its presence in Greenland. It highlights the region's role for digital infrastructure: about 90 percent of Europe-Asia data traffic runs through Red Sea cables, so trans-Arctic cables could reduce latency and redundancy risks. The authors, citing Annegret Bendiek, see an EU Arctic strategy as a way to combine research, infrastructure, security and climate goals with financial backing. They also stress climate risks linked to possible Gulf Stream disruption, which Iceland has classed as a national security threat, and argue that better Arctic early-warning infrastructure would serve all northern states, Europe included. The EU is presenting an updated strategy, replacing a five-year-old paper focused on economics and climate.
brief.argument: The EU needs a security-oriented Arctic strategy that links economic, digital, climate and military interests as the region becomes a geopolitical hotspot.
recommendations: Build trans-Arctic cable infrastructure as an alternative to vulnerable Red Sea routes
Combine research, infrastructure, security policy and climate protection in one EU framework with financial backing
Use Arctic monitoring and early-warning capacity to address Gulf Stream and climate risks

ai.sum: The EU is presenting a new strategy for the Arctic region, reflecting concern over its climate, economic and military significance for Europe.

0af442598c1ac43f.title: Die neuen Sicherheits­partnerschaften der EU
0af442598c1ac43f.summary: Möglichkeiten zur Wahrung von Europas Handlungsfähigkeit in einer imperialen Welt

brief.summary: The authors examine the EU's Security and Defence Partnerships (SDPs), twelve agreements concluded since 2024, as a tool to diversify European security ties amid doubts about US guarantees and great-power rivalry. They assess eight case studies in three circles of partners (EEA and candidate countries, like-minded NATO states, global partners in the Indo-Pacific) plus Türkiye and Ukraine, which lack formal SDPs. The method combines an overview of the instrument with comparative case analysis from the partners' perspective. The SDPs are found to add most value for close non-member states, while their main pull is economic, notably access to SAFE defence financing and trade deals. The authors argue SDPs supplement rather than replace US or NATO commitments, and recommend concrete projects, selective expansion, better intra-EU coordination, and linking bilateral partnerships.
brief.argument: The SDPs are a complementary diversification tool whose value depends on concrete projects, economic incentives such as SAFE access, and better EU-internal coordination rather than on any substitute for US or NATO guarantees.
recommendations: Fill the SDP frameworks with concrete projects and set priorities
Expand the partner circle only selectively
Improve coordination between EU institutions on security partnerships
Link bilateral SDPs into new configurations beyond bilateral formats
brief.turkey: Türkiye is treated as a strategically important partner left without an SDP because the Cyprus dispute blocks deeper security cooperation, so its ties with the EU remain institutionally limited.

ai.sum: An SWP analysis examines the EU’s new security partnerships as a means of preserving its capacity to act in an imperial world.

95045db674c408b6.title: Unpacking MI5’s Warning on a ‘New Era’ of Security Threats
95045db674c408b6.summary: The UK domestic intelligence agency’s annual update rightly focused on a whole-of-society response. But it only scratched the surface of the threat posed by algorithm-driven echo chambers.

brief.summary: The authors, Farah Pandith and Ezra Hess of CFR, respond to MI5 director general Sir Ken McCallum's annual threat update. They praise the speech for centring people, stressing resilience as an everyday practice, calling for a 'team of teams' whole-of-society approach, and recognising the AI threat, including MI5's new AI Threat Assessment Centre. They argue the speech under-described the role of algorithms in building radicalising echo chambers, undersold the vulnerability of young people to online radicalisation, and omitted hate crime, which rose in England and Wales. They conclude that responses must be bespoke, locally rooted and properly resourced, that governments should support parents and communities, and that soft power and social cohesion are linked to national vulnerability.
brief.argument: MI5's threat update was right to frame security as a whole-of-society matter, but it underplayed how algorithm-driven echo chambers and youth radicalisation drive extremism.
recommendations: Build governmental resilience models tailored to different age groups, especially children and adolescents.
Provide infrastructure and support for parents who notice extremist-linked changes in their children.
Fund and partner with local, community-level initiatives through grants and incentives.
Address hate crime explicitly as part of national security resilience.

ai.sum: Analysis of MI5's annual warning on new security threats, arguing its focus on whole-of-society response underplays algorithm-driven echo chambers.

fd1d8464faf1f74c.title: The Missing Pillar of European Resilience
fd1d8464faf1f74c.summary: Social cohesion is the one pillar of the EU's Hybrid Toolbox with no funding of its own. Countering Russian hybrid warfare means building it locally.

brief.summary: The author argues that the EU's Hybrid Toolbox and national strategies concentrate on exposing foreign disinformation and securing infrastructure, but leave social cohesion, the one pillar without dedicated funding, largely unaddressed. Russian hybrid campaigns aim to demoralise European societies and divide communities, and correcting false claims does not touch the grievances that make them believable. Media literacy has value but works slowly and weakly on identity-linked beliefs. The author therefore calls for building cohesion locally: municipalities are presented as more trusted than national governments, and the piece proposes vulnerability mapping, capacity-building for local authorities in tension management, and standing cross-community early response networks. The argument is that such measures are urgent because heightened intergroup threat perceptions can erode cohesion even without direct Russian action.
brief.argument: Europe's resilience to Russian hybrid warfare requires a funded, locally delivered social cohesion pillar, because disinformation alone cannot correct the grievances that hybrid campaigns exploit.
recommendations: Map municipalities where structural vulnerability to tension coincides with active foreign targeting, to direct urgent support
Build a structured capacity-building programme for local governments in mediation, de-escalation, rumour control and recovery planning
Establish Community Early Response Networks with cross-community membership in high-vulnerability municipalities
Give the EU Hybrid Toolbox dedicated funding and programming for community-level social cohesion

ai.sum: Analysis argues social cohesion is the EU Hybrid Toolbox pillar lacking dedicated funding and must be built locally to counter Russian hybrid warfare.

e7920a09e8b318a2.summary: Six candidates are vying to succeed António Guterres as the United Nations’ tenth leader since 1946. Who are they, how are they selected, and what challenges will they face in the role?

brief.summary: The piece is a CFR explainer on the race to succeed António Guterres as UN secretary-general, to take office on 1 January 2027. It profiles six remaining candidates, four of them women, and notes a strong case for a Latin American candidate under informal regional rotation. It explains the selection mechanics: the Charter's bare reference to General Assembly appointment on Security Council recommendation, the nomination and public-dialogue stages introduced in 2016, straw polls, and the nine-vote threshold with no permanent-member veto. The authors argue that the role is formally weak yet influential, and that the next holder will face a liquidity crisis, US funding cuts, UN80 reform, a Security Council they describe as paralysed, and rising security spending pressures among member states. The piece takes no policy position itself.
brief.argument: The authors argue that the 2026 selection will largely follow the 2016 process, and that the next secretary-general will inherit a deeply strained UN facing funding, reform and geopolitical deadlock.

ai.sum: CFR explainer on six candidates vying to succeed António Guterres as UN Secretary-General and selection challenges.

brief.summary: The piece, a set of three Atlantic Council expert analyses, examines how a Lula or Bolsonaro win in Brazil's October 25 runoff would reshape the country's economy, trade and foreign policy. Ambassador James Story argues there is a narrow window for a US-Brazil reset on trade, security and critical minerals, given the right's Senate gains and the threat of a Democratic House after the US midterms. Alejo Czerwonko argues both candidates face the same fiscal imperative of restoring credibility on debt above 80 percent of GDP, differing mainly in pace and spending composition. Valentina Sader argues that either winner must manage US-China competition, Mercosur and Argentina, and a more right-leaning Congress, with Lula favouring diversification and Bolsonaro closer alignment with Washington.
brief.argument: Brazil's October runoff will shape its trade, security, fiscal and regional alignment, but the constraints of fiscal credibility, US-China balance and a more right-leaning Congress limit how far either candidate can shift course.
recommendations: Washington should conclude the critical minerals agreement with Brazil and expand DFC and EXIM financing.
Brazil's next government should establish a durable fiscal anchor to lower interest-rate risk premiums.
Brazil should keep pragmatic trade ties with both the United States and China regardless of the winner.
Any US-Brazil alignment should rest on concrete results such as tariff relief rather than personal affinity, to survive a change in Washington.

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analysis on how a Lula or Bolsonaro win could shape US-Brazil trade, security and critical minerals cooperation.

487265af77d4f8d7.title: The rewiring of globalization is under way
487265af77d4f8d7.summary: Global supply chains are being reconfigured in response to geopolitical and economic upheaval. This is a more nuanced picture than the term "deglobalization" suggests. The post The rewiring of globalization is under way appeared first on Atlantic Council .

brief.summary: The author argues that the world economy is being rewired rather than deglobalised. Trade as a share of GDP rose to over 68 percent in 2025, driven by AI-related goods, critical minerals and services. Trade and investment are increasingly fragmenting along geopolitical lines, with 'friendshoring' among aligned advanced economies. The US share of world trade has slipped slightly while China's trade surplus has grown, prompting talk of a 'China Shock 2.0'. South-South trade is growing quickly and Southeast Asia has become a manufacturing hub. Low-income countries are the main losers, facing weaker trade, lower FDI and aid cuts.
brief.argument: Globalisation is being rewired around resilience and geopolitical alignment rather than collapsing, with gains flowing to countries close to major powers and AI and critical-mineral supply chains.

ai.sum: Atlantic Council analysis argues global supply chains are being reconfigured amid geopolitical upheaval rather than simply deglobalizing.

b6d3cda1d1b17118.title: Establishing Battery Supply Chain Resilience for Drones
b6d3cda1d1b17118.summary: Militaries have spent more than a century operating with fuel and ammunition as limits of combat endurance. They are only beginning to treat batteries with the same operational seriousness, as small unmanned systems move from niche equipment to mass-consumption weapons. Recent bipartisan supply diversification efforts by Congress, the administration, and the Department of Defense provide initial momentum to ensure supply chain independence and resilience for drone…

brief.summary: The authors argue that military drone batteries have become a central constraint on combat endurance, as small unmanned systems move toward mass consumption. They say defence is a price taker in a commercial battery market dwarfed by electric vehicles and grid storage, so it cannot build a purely military ecosystem. Their proposed three-part resilience approach combines a strategic battery reserve, domestic and allied manufacturing with competitive suppliers, and research into new chemistries. They also stress that domestic assembly does not equal supply-chain independence, since Chinese inputs persist deeper in the chain. Tactical charging and power logistics are treated as part of the problem, and the piece urges matching each dependency to consequence and recovery time when choosing between commercial scale, pre-qualified sources, protected capacity, or inventory.
brief.argument: Drone batteries are now a combat-endurance and industrial vulnerability that defence must manage by matching each dependency's consequence and recovery time to the right mix of commercial scale, allied sourcing, protected capacity and strategic reserves.
recommendations: Establish a strategic battery reserve sized to bridge supply interruptions until qualified production is restored.
Standardise battery form factors and interfaces, aggregate military demand, and qualify multiple commercial and allied suppliers.
Protect capacity for high-consequence, slow-recovery dependencies through long-term contracts, capacity reservations or sovereign production.
Fund long-term battery research and government innovation programmes to develop chemistries that reduce exposure to concentrated materials.
brief.turkey: For Türkiye's drone-heavy force planning and defence industry, the piece points to the need to trace battery sub-tier dependencies and to plan for charging and power logistics alongside fuel and munitions.

ai.sum: War on the Rocks article argues militaries must treat drone batteries as a supply-chain vulnerability and calls for diversification.

brief.summary: This is a historical essay by James M. Lindsay of CFR, reconstructing Sunday, 21 October 1962, the sixth day of the Cuban Missile Crisis. Drawing on the day's meetings, it describes Kennedy's sessions with his advisers, including General Sweeney's assessment that an air strike would destroy at most 90 percent of the Soviet missiles. The author recounts how the ExComm debated the wording of the speech, settling on 'quarantine' rather than 'blockade' on Rusk's advice, and narrowing the quarantine to offensive equipment. It also covers the contingency invasion plans, which Kennedy found too slow, and the letters sent to 43 world leaders. The essay ends by noting that the public knew nothing of these deliberations.
brief.argument: Kennedy's choice of 'quarantine' and his narrow initial scope were deliberate diplomatic and political decisions meant to signal resolve while limiting provocation.

a1578c0f0a8649f2.title: Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilians may have a domestic dimension
a1578c0f0a8649f2.summary: Russia's escalating bombing campaign against civilian targets across Ukraine aims to make much of the country unlivable while also serving a propaganda purpose for the Kremlin on the home front, write Syrus Solo Jin and Anton Ponomarenko. The post Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilians may have a domestic dimension appeared first on Atlantic Council .

brief.summary: The authors argue that Russia's sharp escalation of strikes on Ukrainian civilians in 2026 may serve a domestic purpose as well as military and diplomatic ones. With the front largely static and Ukraine regaining ground in some sectors, they suggest civilian infrastructure strikes offer a substitute for battlefield progress. They point to Russian Defense Ministry posts celebrating attacks and to the way strikes are amplified in Russian media, which they say projects military strength and reinforces Putin's narrative of inevitable victory. The rise of Ukrainian drone strikes deep inside Russia, and resulting fuel shortages, add to the pressure. The authors conclude that the campaign is unlikely to be militarily decisive but will probably continue, causing severe hardship to Ukrainians while serving propaganda needs at home.
brief.argument: Russia's escalating strikes on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure may be driven partly by domestic political needs, to create an impression of military strength and progress for a home audience.

0629d813820ade59.title: The withdrawal of the US-led coalition is a loss for Iraq’s sovereignty
0629d813820ade59.summary: The government secured the withdrawal of foreign partners before securing obedience from armed factions. That leaves Baghdad with less leverage against Iran’s allies in Iraq. The post The withdrawal of the US-led coalition is a loss for Iraq’s sovereignty appeared first on Atlantic Council .

brief.summary: The authors argue that the withdrawal of the US-led coalition from Iraq was a genuine act of Iraqi sovereignty, but that it has left Baghdad with less leverage over Iran-aligned armed factions. They describe how groups such as Kataib Hezbollah and Asaib Ahl al-Haq hold formal positions within the Popular Mobilization Forces, keep ties to the IRGC Quds Force, and sustain political and commercial networks that resist government orders. The piece points to Kaabi's flag-trampling video, the postponed weapons-control deadline, and disputes over Iranian flights as evidence of this challenge to Prime Minister Zaidi's authority. The authors contend that the coalition had supplied an alternative to factional security ties, and that its removal raises the stakes of Iraq's dependence on Iranian gas. They call for enforceable disarmament, verified personnel lists, audits of militia-linked contracts, and external support that strengthens state institutions rather than punishing the population.
brief.argument: Iraq's sovereignty over its security will remain incomplete until Baghdad can enforce its decisions against Iran-aligned armed factions that are embedded in state institutions, now that the US-led coalition has departed.
recommendations: Bring heavy weapons into state arsenals under independent inspection to verify disarmament
Tie public salaries to verified personnel lists and obedience to lawful orders
Audit militia-linked contracts and restore state control over border revenues
Diversify energy and electricity links, including with Gulf states, and protect those projects from political interference

ai.sum: Analysis argues Iraq's government secured the US-led coalition's withdrawal before disarming armed factions, weakening its leverage against Iran-aligned groups.

ce9bfea973ff2c5d.title: Washington should stop expecting the Gulf to speak with one voice
ce9bfea973ff2c5d.summary: Gulf states are emerging from the Iran war with different conclusions about how to protect themselves and deal with Tehran. The post Washington should stop expecting the Gulf to speak with one voice appeared first on Atlantic Council .

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Iran war has accelerated existing fractures inside the Gulf Cooperation Council, so Gulf states now reach different conclusions on Iran, defence and diplomacy. Experiences differ sharply: the UAE absorbed far more Iranian strikes than Qatar, reinforcing Abu Dhabi's preference for a decisive outcome and Doha's and Muscat's preference for mediation. The piece holds that Washington keeps expecting the GCC to act as one bloc, treating disagreement as institutional failure rather than geopolitical reality. Using the EU as a model, it urges the US to engage the GCC where interests align and bilaterally where they diverge. It highlights Kuwait, which avoided unilateral moves despite heavy attacks, and the Mecca Agreement among Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, which excludes the UAE.
brief.argument: The Gulf states are diverging on Iran, defence and diplomacy, so Washington should stop treating the GCC as a single strategic actor.
recommendations: Give the GCC the same room for internal disagreement that the EU receives, working through the council where interests align and bilaterally where they do not.
Shorten the path from request to delivery for air and missile defence and counter-drone systems.
Approach co-development with Gulf partners as a strategic investment rather than a concession.
Consult GCC partners early and collectively on any arrangement with Tehran, including missiles, drones and proxies.
brief.turkey: The Mecca Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, under which Türkiye is ready to deploy troops pending parliamentary approval, is cited as evidence of the new Gulf security alignments.

ai.sum: An Atlantic Council analysis says Gulf states are drawing different conclusions from the Iran war on how to deal with Tehran.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Moldova's fight against Kremlin interference faces a test in the November 15 Gagauzia election for governor and People's Assembly. They contend that measures defending the Moldovan state, such as central control of electoral rules and the prosecution of former governor Yevgenia Gutsul, can be recast as attacks on Gagauz self-government, which Moscow exploits. They trace the region's Russian-leaning electoral base to Soviet-era russification and to the 1994 autonomy settlement, whose self-determination clause remains politically potent. The piece presents the Romanian-language candidacy requirement and party exclusions as costly to democratic legitimacy, and treats Turkey as a counterweight to Moscow's claim to protect the Gagauz.
brief.argument: Moldova must enforce electoral integrity against Russian interference in Gagauzia without eroding autonomy and democratic contest, or its countermeasures will feed the grievances Moscow exploits.
recommendations: Harmonise Gagauzia's statute with the national Electoral Code through negotiation rather than litigation.
Support Gagauz language alongside Romanian to show integration need not mean cultural surrender.
Respect the lawful November mandate, including where voters back opponents of the European course.
Have Brussels and Washington co-fund Gagauz language education with Ankara and make EU accession benefits visible in Gagauzia.
brief.turkey: Ankara's consulate, TIKA-funded projects and support for Moldovan territorial integrity give it a role the authors see as a partner in countering Moscow's narrative in Gagauzia.

brief.summary: The article, a War on the Rocks roundtable, examines renewed fighting in Ethiopia's Tigray region after the 2022 peace deal collapsed in September. Five experts were asked to assess risks to Ethiopia, Eritrea, Somalia, Sudan and Egypt. The opening contribution by William Davison argues that state collapse in Ethiopia is unlikely but the most severe risk, in which TPLF resistance could fuel insurgencies in Amhara and Oromia and a rebel march on Addis Ababa. A less dramatic scenario is the federal military becoming bogged down in Tigray with Eritrean backing for the TPLF, weakening government positions elsewhere. The most achievable upside, in his view, would be defeat of the TPLF, which would let Prime Minister Abiy push centralising constitutional reform. The full text beyond the opening is members-only, so the remaining expert views are not available here.
brief.argument: The authors see the Tigray fighting as a serious risk of wider Ethiopian instability and Ethiopia-Eritrea war, with state collapse unlikely but most damaging.

ai.sum: Fighting between Ethiopian forces and the TPLF in Tigray has collapsed the 2022 peace deal and raised spillover risks toward Eritrea.

cb7620c91d07895e.title: Surging Export Similarity is Fueling Advanced Economy Trade Tensions with China
cb7620c91d07895e.summary: Growing global imbalances are only one source of trade frictions with China. Another is the soaring similarity in the export baskets of China and the advanced-economy countries.

brief.summary: The authors argue that trade friction with China is driven not only by aggregate global imbalances but by a rising overlap between China's export basket and that of advanced economies. Advanced economies shifted away from basic manufactures after the first China shock, but since 2016 (chemicals) and 2023 (machinery) the similarity index has climbed steeply, with electric vehicles the largest single driver, lifting Japan and Germany by roughly ten points since 2007. They contend unilateral tariffs are flawed because duties get circumvented, as with plug-in hybrids after the EU's 2024 EV duties, and because overcapacity is merely diverted to third markets. They see the October 7 excess-capacity statement by fifteen economies as a possible path, provided it has agreed triggers, coordinated responses, a credible exit for China verified by members' own monitoring, and an end to threats against partners.
brief.argument: Rising export similarity between China and advanced economies, led by EVs and machinery, makes unilateral tariffs ineffective and requires a coordinated multilateral response to Chinese overcapacity.
recommendations: Adopt a multilateral excess-capacity framework with agreed triggers and coordinated responses to diversion.
Give China a verifiable exit by lifting measures as subsidies are demonstrably cut, judged by members' own monitoring rather than Beijing's reporting.
Stop threatening overcapacity action against partners Washington is courting.
brief.turkey: Türkiye sits outside the advanced-economy core but is exposed to the same diversion of Chinese overcapacity into third markets, so any coordinated trade-defence regime will shape its export access and tariff exposure.

ai.sum: CFR analysis argues rising similarity in China's and advanced economies' export baskets is fuelling trade tensions.

f82e7cdf4bf31861.title: The new Middle East is modular
f82e7cdf4bf31861.summary: In the Middle East today, states are aligning issue by issue, not choosing sides. They cooperate in one area and compete in the next. This modular alignment is shaping the region, even as it manages the shocks of war and energy-market volatility. The post The new Middle East is modular appeared first on Atlantic Council .

brief.summary: The authors argue that the Middle East is not splitting into two blocs but is instead moving toward modular alignment, where states cooperate with the same partners in some sectors while rivaling them in others. They examine the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan-Egypt grouping (the R4) and the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, finding deep bilateral frictions over Libya, Syria, the Eastern Mediterranean and Lebanon. They contend that the UAE-Israel relationship is also case-by-case rather than a bloc, and that economic fragility and divergent priorities undermine binding commitments. The Mecca pact, they say, is far weaker than NATO's Article 5 in practice, and Gulf states increasingly act on their own strategic autonomy, even as they do not break with Washington.
brief.argument: The Middle East is realigning through issue-specific, modular partnerships rather than binding regional blocs, because rivalries and economic constraints prevent members from subordinating their interests.
recommendations: Western capitals should not expect Gulf states to finance regional reconstruction altruistically, since Gulf leaders now invest only where it makes financial sense.
Analysts should judge regional alignments sector by sector rather than as bloc membership.
Mecca Agreement members should build joint infrastructure and binding commitments if they want the pact to function like NATO's Article 5.
brief.turkey: Türkiye's R4 and Mecca Agreement commitments are shallow, and its frictions with Egypt over Libya and gas, and with Saudi Arabia over Syria, mean it should expect cooperation on defence industry and trade rather than a binding alliance.

ai.sum: Atlantic Council argues Middle Eastern states now align issue by issue rather than in fixed blocs.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Trump's unilateral tariff regime faces mounting resistance at home: falling public approval, business and agricultural criticism, and repeated court rulings against his use of emergency trade statutes. They contend that Congress, likely to gain Democratic seats after the midterms, will push bills to reclaim its constitutional trade authority, though such bills would likely be vetoed. They note the bills spare the ten reciprocal trade agreements and that USMCA renewal and a possible Brazil deal are in play. The authors see more durable opportunity in coalitions against Chinese overcapacity and dumping, pointing to the G20 'Milwaukee Framework' on steel and efforts to build critical-minerals supply chains without China. A return to the pre-Trump rules-based WTO order is judged unrealistic during his presidency.
brief.argument: Domestic and legal pushback will constrain Trump's unilateral tariffs, but a return to the old WTO order is unrealistic, so limited liberalisation through coalitions against Chinese overcapacity is the more feasible path.
recommendations: Advanced market economies in North America, Europe and East Asia should deepen cooperation on steel overcapacity and dumping.
Build critical-minerals supply chains that do not depend on China.
Trump should embrace coalitions of willing partners to preserve a reciprocal, balanced trade system.

1f47c11670ceb52c.summary: As Trump’s envoy meets Putin in St. Petersburg, critics accuse the White House of abandoning Ukraine. CFR’s Thomas Graham argues that this criticism may be warranted, but dialogue and diplomacy remain the only route to a settlement that preserves Ukraine’s sovereignty and alignment with the West.

ai.sum: As Trump's envoy meets Putin in St. Petersburg, CFR analysis argues dialogue is the only route to a settlement preserving Ukraine's sovereignty.

brief.summary: The authors argue that criticism of Trump's overtures to Putin may be justified, but outrage does little to clarify the hard choices facing the West and Ukraine. They contend a just peace is unattainable: Russia will keep most seized land and Putin will not face trial, so the realistic aim is an imperfect peace that preserves Ukrainian sovereignty and keeps open Ukraine's path toward European security integration. This requires continued Western weapons and intelligence support, with sanctions judged to have diminishing returns. Dialogue is necessary, and the author sees normalization not as a return to post-Cold War cooperation but as the kind of managed, rivalrous relations that prevailed during the Cold War, with reliable channels to avert crises. Over time, Europe will need deterrence along the frontier, followed by arms control and renewed commercial and societal ties, since Russia and Europe share a continent.
brief.argument: Outrage at Trump's Putin overtures is understandable, but the West should pursue an achievable, imperfect peace that preserves Ukraine's sovereignty and European path, paired with managed dialogue and eventual Cold War-style normalization with Russia.
recommendations: Maintain strong Western military aid and intelligence support to Ukraine to halt or reverse Russian battlefield gains and blunt aerial bombardment
Measure Witkoff's talks against what is achievable rather than against an idealised just peace
Pursue slow integration of Ukraine into European security structures short of NATO membership
Establish reliable channels of communication with Russia and later arms control agreements to prevent escalation

df7f35485af95ad3.summary: Trump and Putin both seem to think that removing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy would set the stage for a Kremlin-friendly peace deal, but most Ukrainians see the war as a fight for national survival that does not depend on any one man, writes Peter Dickinson. ai.sum: An Atlantic Council analysis argues most Ukrainians see the war as national survival rather than loyalty to Zelenskyy.

brief.summary: The author argues that Trump and Putin both wrongly treat Zelenskyy as the main obstacle to peace. He notes that Zelenskyy has accepted every US-backed ceasefire proposal and offered major territorial concessions, while Moscow rejected them. The piece holds that Ukrainians are fighting for national survival rather than for Zelenskyy personally, and that most would resist any replacement pursuing a peace on Russian terms. It describes Putin's rhetoric denying Ukrainian nationhood and the mass detentions and russification in occupied areas as evidence that Ukrainians see the war as existential. The conclusion is that removing Zelenskyy would not change the trajectory of the war, because the resistance rests on collective will rather than one leader.
brief.argument: Ukraine's resistance is driven by an existential fear of Russian annihilation, so replacing Zelenskyy would not produce a Russia-friendly peace.

5e64c3bd2a5276b6.title: Technology , War , and the Limits of Innovation Power in the Middle East

ai.sum: A Washington Institute analysis examines the limits of technology-driven innovation power in the Middle East.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Israel and Iran have each used technological and tactical innovation to achieve results in the 2025 and 2026 wars, but that these gains do not translate into durable strategic outcomes. Israel's model rests on bespoke, intelligence-heavy operations (the pager attacks, targeted strikes, AI-assisted targeting) that are effective in short campaigns but hard to repeat once adversaries adapt. Iran's model relies on cheap, expendable and scalable systems such as Shahed drones, fibre-optic FPV drones used by Hezbollah, and AI-generated propaganda, which impose costs through attrition and asymmetry. The authors contend that the impasse persists mainly for political reasons: Israel has not defined an end state for Gaza, Lebanon or Iran, Iran's IRGC benefits economically from confrontation, and the US lacks durable domestic consensus. Technology alone, they conclude, cannot produce a settlement.
brief.argument: Innovation power yields tactical successes for both Israel and Iran, but without political conditions for a settlement these gains cannot become durable strategic outcomes.
recommendations: Define a durable security architecture for Gaza, including a role for a reformed Palestinian Authority and Arab partners
Pursue a political settlement with Lebanon and a disarmament pathway for Hezbollah
Build an Iran policy designed to outlast a single election cycle
Consolidate military gains through diplomacy, policy and digital public diplomacy, including counters to cheap AI-enabled propaganda
brief.turkey: The piece implies that Türkiye faces a regional environment where cheap drones and AI propaganda lower the cost of coercion, and where Gulf deescalation with Tehran and the Saudi normalisation question shape the broader diplomatic field.

brief.summary: The authors argue that the capture of Ali Kayali (Mihrac Ural), a former pro-Assad militia commander accused of involvement in the 2013 al-Bayda and Baniyas massacres, is welcomed by victims' families but may backfire. Official Syrian media say he was arrested while fleeing across a border, while AFP and Asharq Al-Awsat place the capture inside Lebanon, with a Lebanese source denying prior knowledge and alleging Syrian and Turkish intelligence involvement. The piece contends that if an unauthorised abduction on Lebanese soil is confirmed, it could damage Damascus's efforts to rebuild neighbourly ties and its claimed commitment to the rule of law and sovereignty. Yet, fundamental weaknesses in the North African country’s economy remain, and analysts now wonder how many more shocks it can absorb. Russia’s invasion disrupted global supply chains, so commodity prices soared, including for wheat…

ai.sum: Al Majalla assesses how Egypt's economy absorbed regional shocks better than after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, while weaknesses persist.

brief.summary: The authors argue that Egypt has absorbed the regional shocks from Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the Gaza war and the 2026 US-Iran conflict better than expected, thanks to a large Gulf sovereign injection, about $57bn in total official and bailout funding, rising remittances, and a flexible exchange rate introduced under central bank governor Hassan Abdalla. They credit IMF-linked austerity, tourism and a partial recovery in Suez Canal revenue, and they point to Banque du Caire's planned IPO as a sign that privatisation is resuming. Against this they set a widening current account deficit, heavy reliance on short-term T-bills that crowds out private lending, high borrowing costs, and persistent poverty. The piece concludes that Egypt's stability is real but fragile, and that further regional shocks could test it.
brief.argument: Egypt's economy has weathered regional turmoil better than expected, but deep structural weaknesses, including debt, the current account gap and state dominance, leave it exposed to further shocks.
recommendations: Limit state involvement in the economy and continue privatisation, as the IMF has repeatedly urged.
Maintain the flexible exchange rate to slow the exit of hot money during crises.
Reduce reliance on short-term T-bills so banks can lend more to businesses and debt management improves.
